1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Family-level difference-in-differences (DID) implemented as an event-study.  
Rationale:  
• “Treatment’’ (a sudden, unanticipated hospitalization of one family member) is plausibly exogenous to the future health behaviour of the rest of the family.  
• The panel structure (1997-2011) with precise event dates lets us compare outcomes for relatives before vs. after the index shock, while differencing out calendar-time shocks with date fixed effects and permanent family heterogeneity with family fixed effects.  
• The event-study coefficient path provides an internal pre-trend test and allows the effect to evolve over time (short-run learning vs. long-run behavioural change).  
Because the shock is discrete and timed, DID / event-study dominates IV (no dose–response) and RDD (no running variable).

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
  T_it = 1 for individual i (spouse, child, parent, sibling) in calendar month t that belongs to a family in which another member experienced a first unanticipated hospitalization (index patient excluded).  
Control group  
  All observationally similar individuals in families that have not yet experienced an index hospitalization by month t. They form the counterfactual trend.  
Treatment timing / event date  
  τ_f = calendar month of the first qualifying hospitalization in family f during 1997-2011. The event-study uses k = –24,…, +60 months relative to τ_f (k=0 excluded as baseline).  
Index hospitalization definition  
  • Overnight hospital admission for acute ICD-10 chapters I (circulatory), J (respiratory), K (digestive) or R (symptoms/ill-defined)  
  • No admission for that individual in the previous 24 months.  
Family definition  
  All members linked through the Danish Civil Registration System at τ_f (spouses, cohabitating partners, biological/adoptive children, parents, siblings).  
There is no running variable and cutoff because we are not using RDD.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1 Parallel trends: Absent the index shock, health-care use of relatives in treated families would have trended like relatives in as-yet-untreated families. Plausibility: Universal coverage & rich controls for age, sex, region, and calendar-time shocks make this credible; we will test for parallel pre-trends k<0.  
A2 No differential anticipation: Relatives cannot foresee the unplanned hospitalization far enough in advance to change behaviour. Acute, first-time admissions satisfy this reasonably well.  
A3 No spillovers onto control families: A hospitalization in family A does not directly change behaviour in family B (SUTVA). Population-wide data and large number of families make within-family shocks small enough to ignore between-family spillovers.  
A4 Stable composition: We observe the full population; selective attrition is limited to death/emigration, which we can track and control for.

4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  
Threat 1: Concurrent shocks (e.g., index patient’s death) mechanically alter insurance premiums, bereavement, etc.  
  Remedy: (i) Drop months in which the index patient dies; (ii) estimate separate effects by survival status; (iii) control for family-level income shocks.  
Threat 2: Multiple hospitalizations within the observation window.  
  Remedy: Keep only the first qualifying hospitalization for each family; censor follow-up if a second “index-type” event occurs, or use stacked-event design with robust standard errors clustered at family level.  
Threat 3: Pre-existing but undiagnosed illness in relatives (reverse causality).  
  Remedy: (i) Demonstrate flat pre-trends; (ii) exclude relatives with outpatient visits for the same ICD chapter in the 12 months before τ_f; (iii) placebo shocks assigned to randomly chosen dates.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast IO
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional FE regressions
library(ggplot2)      # plots

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume three CSVs: individuals.csv, hospitalizations.csv, family_links.csv
ind  <- fread("individuals.csv")        # id, sex, yob, region, monthly panel skeleton
hosp <- fread("hospitalizations.csv")   # id, adm_date, icd10, overnight
fam  <- fread("family_links.csv")       # id, family_id (time-invariant for simplicity)

# 2. Define index shocks --------------------------------------------------
hosp <- hosp[overnight == 1]
hosp <- hosp[order(id, adm_date)]
hosp[, lag24 := shift(adm_date, 1), by = id]
hosp[, first24 := (is.na(lag24) | adm_date - lag24 > 730)]   # 730 ≈ 24 months
acute_chapters <- c("I","J","K","R")
hosp <- hosp[substr(icd10,1,1) %in% acute_chapters & first24 == TRUE]

# keep first event for each individual
hosp <- hosp[, .SD[1], by = id]

# 3. Collapse to family index event --------------------------------------
hosp <- merge(hosp, fam, by="id")
# first event per family
hosp <- hosp[order(family_id, adm_date)]
hosp <- hosp[, .SD[1], by = family_id]
hosp[, event_month := as.IDate(cut(adm_date, "month"))]

# 4. Build relative-month panel ------------------------------------------
# Merge family_id & event_month into individual skeleton
ind <- merge(ind, fam, by = "id")

# Add event_month to everyone in the family
ind <- merge(ind, hosp[,.(family_id, event_month)], by="family_id", all.x=TRUE)

# Create relative month k
ind[, calendar_month := as.IDate(month_id)]   # assume month_id exists
ind[, rel_k := as.numeric((calendar_month - event_month)/30.44)]
# Keep window
window <- -24:60
ind <- ind[rel_k %in% window]

# Treatment dummy
ind[, treated_rel := !is.na(event_month) & rel_k >= 0 & id != id_event] # exclude patient
ind[, post := as.integer(rel_k >= 0)]

# Outcome example: monthly GP visits
# Suppose variable gp_visits already in ind
# 5. Main DID w/ event study ---------------------------------------------
ind[, rel_factor := factor(rel_k)]
est <- feols(gp_visits ~ i(rel_k, treated_rel, ref = -1) | id + calendar_month, 
             data = ind, cluster = "family_id")
summary(est)

# Plot coefficients
iplot(est, ci = TRUE) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype="dashed")

# 6. Robustness: placebo dates -------------------------------------------
set.seed(123)
# assign fake event months randomly among control families
placebo <- ind[is.na(event_month)]
placebo_events <- placebo[, .SD[sample(.N,1)], by = family_id][,.(family_id, fake_event = calendar_month)]
placebo <- merge(placebo, placebo_events, by="family_id")
placebo[, fake_rel_k := as.numeric((calendar_month - fake_event)/30.44)]
placebo <- placebo[fake_rel_k %in% window]
placebo[, fake_treat := fake_rel_k >= 0]
placebo[, fake_factor := factor(fake_rel_k)]
placebo_est <- feols(gp_visits ~ i(fake_rel_k, fake_treat, ref = -1) | id + calendar_month,
                     data = placebo, cluster = "family_id")
summary(placebo_est)   # coefficients should be ~0
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic theory: A salient health shock may raise risk salience and increase preventive care among relatives (learning/peer effects). Thus:  
• Short-run (0-6 months): 5–10 % increase in GP visits and prescription fills for cardiovascular medications among spouses and adult children.  
• Medium-run (7–24 months): effect attenuates to ~3 %.  
• Long-run (>24 months): very small or zero.  
In aggregate, total family health-care spending rises modestly, but the improved monitoring is expected to lower emergency admissions of relatives by ~1 p.p. over two years.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
C1 Parallel pre-trends visually & statistically satisfied: 1  
C2 No anticipation evidence (flat −12 to −1 months): 1  
C3 Exogenous timing of acute first hospitalization: 1  
C4 No spillovers to controls (families are separate): 0.5 (some social networks overlap)  
C5 Stable sample composition (attrition controlled): 0.5  
Total = 4/5.
